usecases.title: Run a Hermes agent
usecases.seoTitle: Hermes agent hosting: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I want a personal assistant that answers me on Telegram, remembers what I tell it and runs jobs on a schedule.
usecases.standfirst: Hermes is a personal AI agent you host yourself. It needs a small machine that stays on and keeps its files. Six providers offer it in one click (Agent 37 with no terminal at all; Akamai Cloud, Contabo, DigitalOcean, Hostinger and Vultr as server templates you finish in a terminal); most can run it if you can follow terminal instructions; a few are a poor fit for an assistant that never sleeps.
whatItIs: [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) is an open-source (MIT) assistant from Nous Research. You talk to it from Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, email and [20+ other apps](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/), it keeps a memory of you between conversations, and it writes itself reusable skills from what it does.

The model (Claude, GPT, an open model) runs elsewhere and is billed by its own provider. What you host is the small program that holds your memory, your logins and your schedule, and that runs commands, browses and edits files for you. That program is what this page is about.

Its own README says to run it "on a $5 VPS, a GPU cluster, or serverless infrastructure that costs nearly nothing when idle". A sandbox provider is one of those choices: the difference is how easy it is to set up, whether it is allowed to stay on, and what it costs when it is waiting.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: At least 1 CPU and 1 GB of memory; 2 CPUs and 2 to 4 GB recommended, and at least 2 GB if it uses the browser. 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB leaves room for Chromium and a growing memory.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes, usually. By default it fetches Telegram messages by asking Telegram every few seconds, and the docs say plainly that "a polling bot can never sleep". It also runs your scheduled jobs every 60 seconds. Webhook mode lets it sleep on hosts that wake on an incoming request, but scheduled jobs then do not fire while it sleeps.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Everything in ~/.hermes: memory, past conversations, skills, scheduled jobs, API keys and chat logins. A provider that deletes the disk when the machine stops loses all of it.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: A browser is optional and is the hungriest part. Docker is optional. A GPU is only needed if you run the model yourself.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting. Battleships' modelled always-on assistant workload averages about 6% CPU, with peaks near 100% when it browses or runs a command. That is why providers that charge only for CPU actually used come out cheap here.

twoWays.title: Two ways to use a sandbox with Hermes
body: **Host Hermes on the machine.** Hermes itself lives in the sandbox: it holds your memory, answers your messages and runs around the clock. This is what most people mean, and it needs a provider that lets a machine stay on and keeps its disk.

**Keep Hermes where it is, send its commands to a sandbox.** Hermes runs on your laptop or server, and only the shell commands it decides to run go to a cloud sandbox, so a mistake cannot damage your own machine. Hermes has this built in for [Modal, Daytona and Vercel Sandbox](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration), and Fly.io publishes the same for [Sprites](https://docs.fly.io/sprites/integrations/agent-plugins.md). It is cheap, because the sandbox only runs while a command does, but it is not hosting: your own machine still has to be on.

routes.what: Pick Hermes on the Personal plans and it is set up with a dashboard, task board, web terminal and chat channels. The free plan sleeps when idle; paid plans stay up between scheduled jobs.
routes.price: Personal plans from $3.99 a month; $29.99 with a built-in browser

Nothing preinstalled and no guide. Create a sandbox with auto-stop off, run Hermes' installer over SSH, and keep the gateway running as a service.
Start a sandbox from the dashboard and you get a shell in the browser; install Hermes there and mark the sandbox persistent so it never idle-pauses. No Hermes guide.
The dashboard creates a machine and opens a browser terminal and desktop; installing Hermes and keeping it running is typed by hand. No Hermes template.
The dashboard creates a sandbox and opens a terminal; Hermes is installed by hand. Lizard's one-click templates cover OpenClaw, not Hermes.
Create a Devbox, install Hermes over SSH, and turn on wake-on-HTTP so it pauses between messages and wakes when one arrives.

E2B ships a ready-made hermes template you start from its command line. Sessions end after 24 hours on Pro and one hour on the free plan, so it suits Hermes doing tasks better than an assistant that never stops.

A built-in Hermes backend: Hermes on your own machine starts, stops and resumes a Daytona sandbox for its commands. Daytona's dashboard Playground opens a browser terminal if you want to host it there instead.
A built-in Hermes backend for running its commands. Not an always-on host: Modal sandboxes end after 24 hours and cannot pause.
Vercel publishes an official guide, but it is for the backend mode: Hermes stays on your computer and each task runs in a sandbox.

Fly.io markets Sprites for agents like Hermes, but its only official Hermes integration is the backend mode. Hosting Hermes inside a Sprite means registering it as a service, because a Sprite pauses about 30 seconds after activity stops.
Possible in a sandbox with a volume for its files, installed by hand. Blaxel's agent hosting caps a run at 15 minutes, so it is not the place for an always-on assistant.
Neither Cloudflare nor Hermes documents this. Cloudflare sandboxes also lose their disk when they stop, so memory would have to be saved elsewhere.

Create a named sandbox with `--timeout 0` on Pro, install Hermes and keep it in a background process or under systemd. Suspend is the catch: Hermes polls Telegram every few seconds, so the sandbox has to stay running, and only Pro allows a session with no cap. Everything in `~/.hermes` sits on the ephemeral root disk, so a snapshot or a mounted volume is what saves it if the sandbox is ever terminated.

The Marketplace 'Hermes Agent' image creates a Droplet with Hermes, Node and the OpenAI SDK installed. The listing publishes no post-deploy steps beyond the API example, so expect to add a model key and a channel in the console.

Create a CPX22 (2 vCPU / 4 GB / 80 GB) in the EU, SSH in, install Hermes and run it as a systemd service. The disk, the IP and the process survive, and nothing stops the machine for idleness. Neither Hetzner nor Hermes publishes a Hetzner page; a community Ansible playbook does the provisioning.

The Hermes Agent VPS template deploys the app from the dashboard. You still add a model key and connect Telegram, Discord or another channel from the terminal. Hostinger's separate managed AI automation plan is the no-terminal alternative.

usecases.title: Run an OpenClaw agent
usecases.seoTitle: OpenClaw hosting: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I want OpenClaw answering me on WhatsApp or Slack, with its own browser and memory, without keeping my laptop on.
usecases.standfirst: OpenClaw is a self-hosted assistant built around one always-on gateway. It has more official hosting guides than Hermes: seven providers deploy it in one click, and four more publish a guide or template.
whatItIs: [OpenClaw](https://docs.openclaw.ai/help/faq/what-is-openclaw) is an open-source assistant you run on your own infrastructure, for yourself or a team. It replies on the apps you already use, including WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram, Discord, Signal and iMessage, and can read files, run commands, browse and keep memory.

Its centre is the **Gateway**, which the docs call "the always-on control plane": one long-running program that holds every chat connection and hands messages to the agent. Hosting OpenClaw means hosting the Gateway.

Models run through their own APIs, so no GPU is needed. A team can share one Gateway, but the docs are clear that one Gateway is one trust domain: people who do not trust each other need separate ones.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: At least 1 core, 1 GB of memory and 500 MB of disk; 2 GB or more recommended. OpenClaw's Fly.io guide uses 2 shared CPUs and 2 GB. 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB gives the browser room.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes. The Gateway owns the chat connections, and Telegram uses outbound polling by default. Webhook mode needs a public HTTPS address that is always reachable.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: ~/.openclaw (config, a SQLite database and chat logins) and the agent's workspace (memory and personality files). Lose the WhatsApp credentials and you scan the QR code again.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: A browser is optional; OpenClaw can drive its own Chrome profile. Docker is optional and tool sandboxing is off by default. No GPU for API models.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting: about 6% CPU on average in Battleships' modelled always-on assistant workload, which names OpenClaw, with peaks near 100%.

usecases.title: Give a coding agent its own machine
usecases.seoTitle: Cloud machines for Claude Code and Codex, compared
usecases.question: I want Claude Code or Codex to work on my code in the cloud, not on my laptop.
usecases.standfirst: A coding agent reads a repository, edits files and runs tests. In a sandbox, a mistake cannot touch your laptop, and the work carries on when the laptop is closed. Several providers ship Claude Code and Codex already installed.
whatItIs: Tools like [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) and Codex run in a terminal: you give them a task, they read the code, change it and run commands to check their work. Running them in a cloud sandbox gives each one a disposable Linux machine with your repository on it.
Unlike a personal assistant, a coding agent does not need to stay on. It runs while you work and can stop at night, as long as the repository, its caches and the agent's login survive.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Claude Code needs 4 GB of memory or more. Anthropic's own cloud sessions allow up to about 4 vCPU, 16 GB and 30 GB of disk. 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 40 GiB covers the agent, tests and a few containers.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. It runs during working hours; this guide assumes eight hours on 20 days, 160 hours a month.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The repository and uncommitted work, the agent's login (~/.claude for Claude Code), and caches and Docker images if you want a fast start.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: Docker helps when tests need databases or services. A browser matters only for checking web interfaces. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting on the model: about 4% CPU on average in Battleships' modelled software-factory workload, with short peaks during builds.

usecases.seoTitle: Code interpreter sandboxes for your product, compared
usecases.question: My app lets users or an LLM run code, and I need somewhere safe to run it.
usecases.standfirst: A code interpreter is a sandbox your application calls: send code, get back the output, the errors and any files. Each run is short and thrown away, so the price of a second of compute, how quickly a sandbox starts and how many can run at once matter more than anything else.
whatItIs: This is infrastructure you build into a product, not something your users log into. Your server asks the provider's API for a sandbox, runs the code, collects the result and throws the sandbox away.

The code is untrusted by definition, so isolation is the first question: whether each run gets its own kernel, and what it can reach on the network. The [isolation](/features/isolation/) and [outbound network](/features/outbound-network/) pages compare that.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. Each run lasts seconds to minutes. This guide's example is 20,000 one-minute runs a month, about 650 a day (Battleships models 200,000 sessions).

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Usually nothing. Results go back to your app or your own storage.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: About 17% CPU on average in Battleships' modelled interpreter workload. Charging by the second, and only for CPU actually used, both matter here.

usecases.title: Host your own n8n
usecases.seoTitle: n8n hosting: where to self-host n8n and what it costs
usecases.question: I want n8n running my automations around the clock, on a server I control, without paying per workflow run.
usecases.standfirst: n8n is a visual automation tool you can host yourself. It needs a small machine that never sleeps and keeps its database. Four providers set it up in one click and OVHcloud ships it preinstalled; most others can run it if someone follows terminal steps; the task-only sandboxes are the wrong place for it.
whatItIs: [n8n](https://docs.n8n.io/) is a workflow automation tool. You draw a workflow on a canvas: a **trigger** (something that starts it, such as a form being sent or a time of day), then steps that call other apps, reshape data or ask an AI model. Its [README](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n) counts 1,500+ ready-made connections.

Hosting it yourself means you run the server, its database, its encryption key and its upgrades. In return there is no per-run fee: n8n's own hosted [n8n Cloud](https://n8n.io/pricing/) is billed by how many workflow runs you use.

Most workflows start in one of two ways: a **webhook**, which is a web address another app calls when something happens, or the [Schedule Trigger](https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/core-nodes/n8n-nodes-base.scheduletrigger), n8n's own built-in clock. Both only work while n8n is running, which decides what kind of machine it needs.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: n8n publishes no self-hosting minimum. Its Cloud plans run from 640 MiB of memory to 4 GiB, and the software alone uses about 180 MiB. Because any single step can pull a large file into memory, 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB is the safer buy.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes. n8n listens for webhooks only while it runs, and the Schedule Trigger works "in a similar way to the Cron software utility": its clock lives inside the machine. A sleeping machine misses both. A host that wakes on a web request can still catch webhooks after a short delay, but scheduled runs will not fire while it sleeps.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The database (workflows, saved logins to other apps, run history; SQLite by default, PostgreSQL for anything larger) and the encryption key n8n creates on first start. Without that key the saved logins cannot be read, and a database backup alone will not bring them back.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: No browser on the server: the editor opens in yours. The documented install uses Docker (a standard way to package and run software); npm on Node.js 20.19 to 24.x is the alternative. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting. No benchmark measures n8n; Battleships' nearest modelled always-on workload averages about 6% CPU, with peaks near 100% when a large workflow runs. Size for the peak, not the average.

routes.what: A Deploy Now template creates an n8n app and a separate managed PostgreSQL database, connects them and gives n8n a public HTTPS address. It does not set an encryption key, attach a volume or add worker processes.

usecases.title: Host your own Discord or Slack bot
usecases.seoTitle: Discord and Slack bot hosting: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I wrote a bot that answers questions in our Discord or Slack using an AI model, and I need somewhere for it to live.
usecases.standfirst: A chat bot is a small program that waits for messages, asks a model and replies. How Discord or Slack delivers those messages decides whether it can ever sleep. No provider hosts your own bot in one click; one provider's guide stands out, and the task-only sandboxes are a poor fit.
whatItIs: A support or community bot holds a login token for the chat app, receives each message, assembles some context, calls a model and posts the answer. You write it with a library such as [discord.js](https://github.com/discordjs/discord.js) or Slack's Bolt; the model runs elsewhere and is billed by its own provider.

Discord bots normally keep a **WebSocket** open to Discord: a connection that stays open so messages can be pushed down it at any moment. Discord calls these [persistent connections](https://discord.com/developers/docs/topics/gateway) that the bot must keep alive with regular heartbeats. Slack offers the same in [Socket Mode](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-socket-mode).

The other way is a public web address that Discord or Slack calls for each message ([Slack Request URLs](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-http-request-urls), [Discord interactions](https://discord.com/developers/docs/interactions/overview)). A bot built that way only needs to be awake when a message arrives. A bot that reads every message in a server needs the open connection, and so a machine that stays on.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Neither Discord nor Slack publishes one. 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 10 GiB runs Node or Python, a small history database and one model call at a time, with room for logs. Battleships models this job at 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes for a bot with an open connection: if it misses a heartbeat, Discord closes the connection, and a bot may only log in to it 1,000 times a day, so a host that keeps sleeping and waking it is a bad host. A bot that only answers through a web address can sleep if the host wakes it on a request.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The bot token (anyone with it controls the bot), conversation history and any settings. Lizard's guide keeps them in a database rather than the machine's disk, and warns to run only one copy per token, or every copy answers every message.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: No browser. Docker is optional. A database is recommended for history; SQLite (a single-file database) is enough for one copy. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Idle almost all the time, busy in short bursts when a message arrives. Battleships' modelled always-on assistant averages about 6% CPU; one community server sees less traffic, so the calculator uses 3%.

usecases.title: Give a small team Claude Code in the cloud
usecases.seoTitle: Claude Code in the cloud for a team: setup and costs
usecases.question: Three to five of us want Claude Code running on cloud machines, each with our own login, without sharing one account.
usecases.standfirst: Claude Code is built for one person on one machine. For a team that means one machine per developer, each signed in with that developer's own account. Six providers ship it preinstalled and one sets it up in one click; the catch is how logins are kept.
whatItIs: [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview) is Anthropic's coding agent. A developer starts it in a repository and asks for a change; it reads and edits files and runs commands and tests on the machine where it runs.

Vercel's guide puts the hosting constraint plainly: Claude Code "isn't built to be safe for multiple tenants: it's a command-line tool for one user, it keeps its state on disk" ([Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/agent-harnesses/claude-code)). A shared machine would hold one person's login and mix everyone's unfinished work, so the default is one machine each.

For a team, three things have to be decided together: where each copy runs, whose Claude account pays, and what survives when a machine is replaced. The machine does not need to stay on; it runs while people work.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Anthropic asks for 4 GB of memory or more and gives no CPU or disk minimum. Its own cloud sessions allow 4 vCPU, 16 GB and 30 GB of disk. 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 40 GiB per developer covers the agent, tests and a few containers, with room for their images.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. Each machine runs during working hours: eight hours on 20 days is 160 hours each, or 800 for five developers. It can stop between sessions if its disk survives.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The repository and any work not yet pushed, and the login: on Linux, ~/.claude/.credentials.json. If the disk is thrown away, the developer signs in again and unpushed work is lost.

needs.label: Whose login
needs.value: On Claude's Team plan, "team members install Claude Code and log in with their claude.ai accounts", so each machine holds its owner's login. Some platforms store one Claude login for the whole account, which every sandbox uses: convenient alone, wrong for a team that wants usage and access per person.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting on the model: about 3% CPU on average in Battleships' modelled software-factory workload, with peaks near half the machine during builds and tests.

routes.what: The agent37-claude-code template sets up one Claude Code instance on the developer's own Anthropic account. One instance each, so five developers means five; team management and roles are on the Max plan.

usecases.title: Run a scraper on a schedule
usecases.seoTitle: Run a scraper on a schedule: the cheapest cloud options
usecases.question: I want a script that checks a few websites four times a day and saves what it finds, without paying for a machine that sits idle.
usecases.standfirst: A scheduled scraper runs for minutes a day and is idle the rest. What matters is where the schedule lives and where the results go, not the machine. A schedule inside a sleeping machine does not fire, so look for providers whose platform starts the run.
whatItIs: A scraper fetches a set of pages, picks out the fields you care about (prices, listings, headlines) and writes them to a file or database. Pages that build themselves with JavaScript need a **headless browser**, a real browser such as Chromium running without a screen, driven by a tool like [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro). Plain pages only need a download.

The schedule is usually written as a **cron** expression, a short line such as "run at 6, 12, 18 and 24 o'clock" named after the Unix tool that runs jobs on a timetable. The key question is who keeps that clock. Agent 37 says it directly: "a crontab inside the container only runs while the container is running" ([Agent 37](https://www.agent37.com/docs/agents-api/crons)).

So there are two designs: a scheduler run by the platform that starts a fresh machine for each run (cheap), or a machine that stays on all month with its own timer (simple, and billed around the clock).

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: No vendor publishes one. 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 10 GiB fits a headless browser and logs; Battleships models one browser visit at 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 5 GiB. Plain downloads fit in 1 GiB.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No, if the schedule lives outside the machine. Four ten-minute runs a day is about 20 machine-hours a month, not 730. A timer inside the machine only works if the machine stays on.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The results, kept outside the run: Runtime's jobs, for example, start "a fresh sandbox" every time and tell you to put data on a volume. Also cookies if a site needs a login, and a marker of what was already saved so a rerun does not duplicate rows.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: A browser only for pages built with JavaScript; it is the largest memory cost. Docker is optional. A database is optional on the machine but needed somewhere. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Busy while a run is open: about 40% CPU in Battleships' modelled scraping workload, because a browser does real work. Idle for the rest of the day.

routes.what: Lizard's sandboxes have no scheduler, but its one-click n8n template gives you n8n's Schedule Trigger and a PostgreSQL database for the results. Build the scrape as a workflow.
The best fit among the sandboxes: a schedule in a script, and the platform "wakes a sleeping machine, on standby or hibernated, shortly before" it is due. A missed slot runs once on wake.
Scheduled jobs run a command in a fresh sandbox on a cron, keep its output and exit code, and show up on a Jobs page in your account. Results go to a volume or your own storage.
The schedule is a Workers feature, Cron Triggers: the scheduled Worker can start a sandbox for the scrape. Each run gets up to 15 minutes of CPU on the paid plan.
Vercel Cron Jobs call a function, which can start a sandbox. The free Hobby plan runs crons only once a day, which is too rare here; Pro allows once a minute.

Platform crons fire "whether the instance is awake or asleep", but they wake an agent and give it a prompt, and are not offered on the base or n8n templates. For a script, the n8n template with auto-sleep off is the other route.
A schedule attaches to a Modal function written in code; the function can do the scrape or start a sandbox.
Sandbox schedules run a command inside a sandbox on a cron, with a run history; up to 100 per sandbox. Set up from code or the API.
No scheduler. A timer inside a machine left on works, but the machine is billed all month; otherwise something outside has to start a sandbox per run.
No scheduler found. A scheduler of your own calls Daytona's API to create a sandbox for each run.
No scheduler found. E2B is driven from code, so the schedule lives in your app or another service.
No scheduler found. A machine wakes on an API call or a visit to its public address, so an outside scheduler can start each run.
No scheduler found. An outside scheduler can wake a Devbox with a web request, but its own clock stops while it is paused.
No scheduler found. Idle pause and auto-stop are adjustable, so an outside scheduler plus the API is the route.
No scheduler found. The Tasks API keeps a Sprite awake during a run, but something outside has to start it.
cron inside a Droplet that stays on. DigitalOcean has no scheduler that starts a machine, so the idle hours between runs are billed at the full rate.

Run the schedule inside the server with cron or a systemd timer, and write results to Object Storage or a volume so they outlive the machine. A fresh server per run is possible but every run under an hour is billed as a full hour, so an always-on small server is usually cheaper.
routes.price: 120 ten-minute runs × 1 h × $0.0216 ≈ $2.59 + $0.12 IPv4, against $14.09 for an always-on CPX12

routes.what: Run the scraper from cron inside the VPS. Four ten-minute runs a day is only about 20 machine-hours a month, but the VPS plan bills all 730 hours: KVM 1 costs $19.49 either way. Store results outside the VPS if it may be deleted.
No scheduler. Trigger the run from your own cron or queue, create an ephemeral VM, scrape, write results to external storage, and let the VM delete itself.
routes.price: $0 on Free at 120 ten-minute runs a month, inside the monthly allowances.

routes.what: Cron inside the VM runs the scraper four times a day, but a monthly plan bills the 700+ idle hours too. It only makes sense if the same box does other work; otherwise a per-task sandbox is cheaper.
routes.price: $5.72/mo (VPS XS) whatever the run count, ex-VAT

routes.what: Run the scraper from cron or a systemd timer inside the guest. The VPS bills all month, so a ten-minute nightly scrape still costs $5.35; store results in Object Storage or somewhere outside the machine if it may be rebuilt.

Run cron or a systemd timer inside a Small-2GB instance. The machine has to exist all month, so four ten-minute runs a day cost the full monthly price rather than twenty minutes of compute; write results to object storage or an external database before the instance is replaced.
A cron schedule invokes a deployed Tensorlake application, which can start a sandbox for each scrape; the schedule lives outside the sandbox, and results need a volume or your own storage.

Run cron or a systemd timer inside an always-on instance, or create a fresh instance per run through the API. A fresh 1 vCPU / 2 GiB instance is billed a whole hour per run, so 120 ten-minute runs cost about $1.79 against $10 for an always-on box; write results to Object Storage.

Run cron or a systemd timer inside Cloud VPS 4. The schedule works because the machine never sleeps, but 20 hours of scraping a month costs the same as 730 because there is no hourly meter and a stopped server still bills.
Cron inside a Linode that stays up. Four ten-minute runs a day bill the full $24 month, because a powered-off Linode bills in full and a deleted one loses the cron and the disk.

Run the schedule inside a small always-on DEV1-S with cron or a systemd timer, and write results to Object Storage so they outlive the machine. A fresh machine per run is possible but every ten-minute run bills a full hour of compute, disk and IPv4; at DEV1-S rates that is still cheap, but the machine must be created and deleted by your own code.
routes.price: 120 ten-minute runs ≈ $2.04; an always-on DEV1-S is $12.41 a month

picks.watch: The schedule is written as a script file, and the $30 of starting credit needs a card.

picks.why: Scheduled jobs start a clean sandbox on a cron and keep each run's output on a Jobs page. CPU is billed only while it works: about $0.50 a month here.
picks.watch: Nothing on a job's own disk survives the run; save results to a volume or your own database. One US region.

usecases.title: Host your own MCP server
usecases.seoTitle: Host a remote MCP server: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I built tools for Claude as an MCP server, and I want it at a web address so Claude can use them without anything running on my laptop.
usecases.standfirst: A remote MCP server is a small web service that gives an AI client your tools. It needs a public HTTPS address that answers, and very little else. One provider deploys one in a click, a few publish guides, and several providers' own MCP servers are something else entirely.
whatItIs: The [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports) (MCP) is how AI apps such as Claude find and use outside tools: search your documents, file a ticket, query a database. An **MCP server** is the program that offers those tools.

A local server runs on your own computer, started by the app. A remote one runs at a web address and speaks "Streamable HTTP", so Claude or [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp) can connect from anywhere. Claude's guide says a remote server "runs on infrastructure you host and is reachable over the internet" ([Claude](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building)).

Watch the wording on provider sites. Daytona, Sprites, Runtime and E2B all document MCP servers, but theirs let an AI agent control their sandboxes, or run MCP tools privately for your own agent. They are not a way to host your server for Claude.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: No vendor publishes one. A server whose tools call other services is a small web process: 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 10 GiB covers it, logs and an optional session store. A server whose tools run code or a browser should be sized like that work.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: It must answer whenever the client calls. A host that sleeps can work if it wakes on the incoming request: Lizard's guide sleeps after 10 quiet minutes, and the first call afterwards takes longer. Claude allows 240 seconds per tool call.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Usually nothing: Cloudflare's template builds a fresh server for each request. If you use OAuth (a standard sign-in so only allowed users can connect), the signing keys and registered clients must survive, or every client has to sign in again.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: No browser unless a tool drives one. Docker is optional. A database only if a tool needs one, and it can live elsewhere. No GPU: the model runs on the client's side.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Idle between tool calls and busy for milliseconds during one. There is no benchmark for it; the calculator uses 2%, below Battleships' modelled 6% for an always-on agent, because the server only passes calls on.

A public port works and wakes a paused machine, but published ports have no login: "anyone can reach the whole service". Put the access check in the server. No MCP guide.

Runtime's catalogue MCP servers run at private addresses for your own agent. Hosting yours for Claude is a normal sandbox with a custom domain; no guide.
No MCP template. A custom image can run the server, and every port gets a public agent37.app address. No MCP guide.
Daytona's own MCP server lets an AI agent control Daytona sandboxes. Hosting your own server is a manual install with no guide.
E2B's MCP gateway runs MCP tools inside a sandbox for your agent, which is the opposite direction. Sessions also end after one or 24 hours.
Sprites publishes a remote MCP server for controlling Sprites. Hosting yours means a service on a port, which wakes on a request; no guide.
A sandbox port gets a public address, but sandboxes are made for one task and end; a Vercel Function would be the simpler host. No MCP guide.
A small Droplet with a public IPv4 answers at a stable address all month. DigitalOcean's own MCP server manages DigitalOcean resources; it does not host your server.

Create a CPX02 (1 vCPU / 1 GB / 20 GB) with a Primary IP and a Cloud Firewall rule for the port, then run the MCP server as a service. It must stay up, because a powered-off server cannot be woken by an incoming request.

Run a small HTTP MCP server on KVM 1, with systemd and a TLS reverse proxy such as Caddy or Traefik. The public IPv4, root access and always-on plan make it a straightforward fit; you own authentication and certificate renewal.
Run your MCP server in a VM and route a style.dev domain to its port; forward auth can gate it. There is no MCP template and no MCP server for controlling Freestyle.

routes.what: VPS Nano is the cheapest always-on public address in this guide: point DNS at the IPv4, open the port in the panel firewall and terminate TLS yourself. Nothing sleeps it, so a client's tool call never waits for a wake.

A public IPv4, any TCP port and root make a VPS-1 a natural home for a remote MCP server. Install the server, put TLS in front with Caddy or Traefik, and add authentication yourself; there is no private URL or OAuth layer.

Run the MCP server on a Micro-1GB instance behind Caddy for TLS, with a static IP and a firewall rule for 443. This is a good fit: a small always-on process, a fixed address and 2 TB of transfer for $7 a month.

routes.what: No MCP guide or template. A named sandbox can run the server and expose its port at a public sandbox URL, but it suspends after ten quiet minutes, so an idle server wakes on the next call.
Vultr's MCP guide runs a FastMCP server on an Ubuntu instance and reaches it over HTTP; add TLS and authentication yourself. The instance needs a public IPv4 and must stay up.

Run your MCP server on Cloud VPS 4 behind its public IPv4. The machine stays up, so the client always reaches it; TLS and authentication are yours to add, and there is no MCP-specific tooling from Contabo.

Run the MCP server on the Nanode 1 GB ($5) or Linode 2 GB ($12), put Caddy in front for TLS, and use the free DNS Manager and Cloud Firewall. The server answers all month because nothing idles the machine.
